replies:
**Yes, absolutely.** Screening for hepatitis B is a routine, essential part of first-trimester prenatal care, and every major health organization (including the CDC, ACOG, and WHO) recommends it for all pregnant people — not just those with risk factors.

Here’s why it matters and what you can expect:

### Why screening is so important
- **Mother-to-child transmission is highly preventable** — but only if we know your status. If you have hepatitis B, the virus can pass to your baby during birth. Without intervention, up to 90% of infected babies develop chronic hepatitis B, which can lead to serious liver problems later in life.
- **Timely treatment is extremely effective.** If you test positive, your baby can receive two shots within 12 hours of birth — hepatitis B immune globulin (HBIG) and the first dose of the hepatitis B vaccine. This combination reduces the risk of transmission to less than 5%.
- **It’s a silent infection.** Many people with chronic hepatitis B have no symptoms and feel perfectly healthy, so only a blood test can tell.

### What the test involves
It’s a simple blood draw that looks for the **hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg)**. It’s often bundled with other routine prenatal labs (like HIV, syphilis, blood type, etc.), so you likely won’t even need an extra needle stick.

### What if it comes back positive?
- It does **not** mean your baby will get hepatitis B — it means you and your medical team can take the necessary steps to protect them.
- You’ll be offered follow-up testing and may be referred to a specialist to monitor your own liver health during and after pregnancy.
- Your newborn will get those two protective shots right after birth, which is incredibly effective.

### If you’ve been vaccinated
You still need the test. The vaccine is excellent, but no vaccine is 100% effective. The screening checks for current infection, not immunity. Your provider may also check your immunity level (anti-HBs) if there’s a chance your protection has waned.

### The bottom line
This is a universal, low-risk, high-reward screening. It’s one of the simplest things you can do right now to give your baby a healthy start. At your first prenatal visit, your provider will almost certainly offer it — but if for any reason they don’t bring it up, feel free to ask for it explicitly.

Congratulations on your pregnancy! This is a great example of you already advocating for yourself and your little one. You’re doing the right thing by asking.
DO IT. Screening is universally recommended, and it's a simple step to protect your baby from a preventable infection.
